subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: The big idea of this unit is a lovely surprise: computers are not only the big screen on a desk or the tablet in your hand — tiny computers hide inside all sorts of everyday things, and they are the boss. A washing machine, a microwave, a fridge and even some toys have a little computer inside. We cannot see it, but it is there, and it controls the machine — it tells the machine what to do. The word for that is control, and it is the heart of the whole unit. First, that some everyday devices use computers — and what each hidden computer controls (the fridge computer keeps our food cold, the microwave computer sets the cooking time). Second, what a robot is — a machine with a computer inside that can do a job all by itself, with no person helping. You learn the happy, important truth that a robot is a machine, not a person: it cannot feel sad or happy. Third, that computers give us information back, called output — and the output devices that show it to us: a speaker to hear, a screen to see, a printer to put words and pictures on paper.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 1 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Know that some everyday devices have a computer inside them (a washing machine, a microwave, a fridge, some toys).
Say that the computer controls the device — it tells it what to do — and give one example ("the fridge computer keeps our food cold").
Sort simple things into has a computer and no computer.
Say what a robot is: a machine that does a job by itself, with no help from a person.
Know that a robot is not alive and cannot feel happy or sad.
Name one place a robot works (a factory, a dangerous job, or a place people cannot go, like Mars).
Know that a robot that looks like a person is called an android.
Know that computers give us output, and match an output device to its job (a speaker to hear, a screen to see, a printer to put on paper).

concepts.title: Computers hide inside things
concepts.explanation: Lots of everyday things have a computer hiding inside them. We cannot always see it, but it is there. The computer controls the thing — it tells the thing what to do. We know a tablet is a computer. But here is a secret — a tiny computer also hides inside a washing machine!
concepts.example: We cannot see it, but it is there, and it is the boss. It controls the machine.
concepts.checkYourself: it keeps the food cold. Can you name a device and say a computer is hidden inside it?

concepts.title: Which things have a computer?
concepts.explanation: Not everything has a computer. Plain, simple things — a ball, a spoon, a book — have no computer. We can sort things into two groups: has a computer and no computer. Put out two boxes or two hoops, one labelled has a computer and one no computer.
concepts.example: Answer this in your own words, out loud or on paper: Which things have a computer? Then check your answer against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a spoon has no computer but a washing machine does? Can you sort a simple thing from a computer thing?

concepts.title: Meet the robots
concepts.explanation: A robot is a machine with a computer inside that can do a job all by itself, with no person helping. A robot is not a person. A robot cannot feel happy or sad. A robot that looks like a person is called an android — but most robots do not look like people at all. A robot is a machine that does a job by itself. It has a computer inside, and the computer controls it.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: meet the robots. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand a robot cannot feel? Can you name one place a robot works?

concepts.title: Output: how computers tell us things
concepts.explanation:
A computer gives us information back. That is called output. Output is something we can see, hear or feel. We get it through an output device: a speaker to hear, a screen to see, a printer to put words and pictures on paper.

Leo's friends sent him some things. Grace sang a song and sent it. Nadia wrote a letter.
concepts.example: Sami sent some pictures. Which output device does Leo use for each one?
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that output can be heard, not only seen? Can you match a job — hear a song, see a picture, put it on paper — to the right output device?

concepts.title: Design and build a robot: the Mini-Project
concepts.explanation: This session and the Mini-Project sheet go hand in hand. You are going to make your very own robot! First, think — what job will your robot do? Maybe it cleans the floor, waters the plants, or helps in the kitchen. Then we build it from boxes and tubes.
concepts.example: Then we choose its output — does it have a screen? a speaker? a flashing light? Then we show everyone.
concepts.checkYourself: Did you build something and name it? Did you enjoy sharing it? Do you give your robot a clear job?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

commonMistakes: A computer is only a laptop or a tablet.
Tiny computers also hide inside many everyday things — the washing machine, the microwave, some toys. We just cannot see them.
Anything that turns on has a computer.
Not true. A plain torch or a light bulb has no computer — it only makes light. A computer is the clever part that follows steps and controls the machine.
a robot can feel happy or sad.
No. A robot is a machine. It cannot feel anything. It only does the job its computer was given.
The computer thinks for itself and decides what to do.
No. The computer only follows the steps that people gave it. People are always the boss.
All robots look like metal people.
Most robots do not look like people at all. A robot that looks like a person is called an android; many robots look like an arm, a box, or a little car.
Output means only pictures on a screen.
Output can be things we hear, from a speaker, and things we hold, from a printer — not only things we see.

selfAssessment: I can know that some everyday devices have a computer inside them (a washing machine, a microwave, a fridge, some toys).
I can say that the computer controls the device — it tells it what to do — and give one example ("the fridge computer keeps our food cold").
I can sort simple things into has a computer and no computer.
I can say what a robot is: a machine that does a job by itself, with no help from a person.
I can know that a robot is not alive and cannot feel happy or sad.
I can name one place a robot works (a factory, a dangerous job, or a place people cannot go, like Mars).
I can know that a robot that looks like a person is called an android.
I can know that computers give us output, and match an output device to its job (a speaker to hear, a screen to see, a printer to put on paper).
